# Who Yields to Whom? Corridor Behavior Around Autonomous Linen Carts

## Summary

This analysis examines whether an autonomous linen cart’s stopping distance affects how often older residents hesitate or change course during corridor encounters. Data came from two residential care facilities operated by Northmere Living, where Morrow linen carts make scheduled trips between laundry rooms and household units.

Across 10,472 usable encounters, residents showed a defined hesitation response in 24.7% of encounters under the cart’s standard 1.2-metre yielding rule and 18.0% under an early-yield rule that stopped the cart 2.4 metres away. The reduction was largest among residents using walkers. Early yielding also reduced turn-backs, but it increased the time carts spent obstructing some doorways.

The results support using early yielding at open corridor intersections, especially on floors with many walker users. They do not establish that the same setting is appropriate near doors, lifts, or in facilities with different layouts.

## Data and outcome definitions

The study covered eight weeks in spring at Northmere’s Alder Quay and Brindle House facilities. Each building had three participating floors and one Morrow cart. Firmware alternated between two modes by calendar day:

- **Standard yield:** stop when a resident was detected within 1.2 metres of the projected route.
- **Early yield:** stop at 2.4 metres and remain stationary until the route was clear.

The alternating schedule was chosen so that both modes would operate on weekdays and weekends. It was not concealed from staff, and facilities could override the assigned mode when moving unusually large loads.

Seventy-three residents who routinely used shared corridors wore location badges during the study. Encounters were formed by matching badge positions to cart lidar logs. An encounter began when a resident and cart came within four metres while moving toward the same intersection or toward each other.

The primary outcome was a **hesitation response**, defined as either a pause of at least two seconds or a lateral movement of more than 0.6 metres within five seconds of the cart entering the four-metre zone. A **turn-back** occurred when the resident reversed direction and travelled at least two metres. These measures describe movement, not the resident’s emotional state.

The logs contained 12,418 candidate encounters. We excluded 1,143 because the badge signal disappeared for more than two seconds, 526 because a staff member was manually driving the cart, and 277 because furniture or a service trolley blocked the lidar view. This left 10,472 encounters: 5,284 in standard mode and 5,188 in early-yield mode.

## Results

| Mobility aid recorded in care profile | Encounters | Standard hesitation | Early-yield hesitation | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| None | 4,116 | 18.6% | 14.9% | -3.7 points |
| Cane | 1,942 | 24.8% | 18.2% | -6.6 points |
| Walker | 3,476 | 33.4% | 22.1% | -11.3 points |
| Wheelchair | 938 | 16.2% | 14.7% | -1.5 points |
| **All encounters** | **10,472** | **24.7%** | **18.0%** | **-6.7 points** |

In a logistic regression adjusting for building, hour of day, intersection, and mobility-aid category, early yielding was associated with lower odds of hesitation (odds ratio 0.66; 95% confidence interval 0.60–0.73). The model treated encounters as observations and used standard errors clustered by calendar day.

Turn-backs declined from 3.8% of standard-mode encounters to 2.6% under early yielding. The absolute difference was modest, equivalent to approximately one fewer turn-back per 83 encounters. There were no recorded collisions in either mode, so the data cannot show whether stopping earlier changes collision risk.

The association was strongest from 7:00 to 10:00, when breakfast traffic and linen deliveries overlapped. Hesitation fell by 9.4 percentage points in that period, compared with 4.1 points after 18:00. This pattern may mean that early yielding is most helpful in busy corridors, although it could also reflect different residents using the corridors at different times.

A restricted calculation using no more than one randomly selected encounter per resident per day produced a 5.9-point reduction. This is smaller than the main estimate but points in the same direction.

## Classification check

To test the automated outcome, two analysts independently reviewed 240 short, silent clips selected from common-area cameras. Against their reconciled labels, the movement rule had 86% precision and 79% recall for hesitation. Agreement between reviewers was 88% before reconciliation.

The validation clips were disproportionately from daytime encounters because several night cameras did not retain sufficient detail. Walker users were also easier to classify than residents walking without aids: the frame of a walker made pauses and lateral movements more visible. Some of the apparent difference between mobility groups could therefore come from measurement performance.

## Operational trade-offs

Early yielding added a median of 4.1 seconds to each cart encounter. Over a typical 46-encounter day, this represents about three additional stationary minutes. Total route completion time increased by 2.8%, which did not cause any scheduled linen run to be cancelled.

However, a cart stopped within a marked doorway clearance zone in 7.9% of early-yield encounters, compared with 4.2% in standard mode. Review of maintenance notes suggested that the cart sometimes detected a resident through an open doorway and stopped before fully clearing the entrance. Staff submitted nine obstruction reports during early-yield days and three during standard days. These counts are small and reporting was informal, but they identify a practical cost not captured by the hesitation outcome.

## Interpretation and recommendation

The observed pattern is consistent with residents benefiting when a robot makes its intention to yield earlier. The particularly large difference for walker users is operationally important because they accounted for one-third of encounters and had the highest baseline hesitation rate. A stationary cart at greater distance may provide more room to maintain a straight path without negotiating which party will move first.

Northmere should retain the 2.4-metre rule at open intersections for a three-month trial and prioritize floors with high walker use. Door approaches should instead use a location-specific rule that allows the cart to clear the doorway before stopping. Route completion time, obstruction reports, and resident turn-backs should all be monitored rather than treating hesitation as the sole success measure.

The evidence is not a clean randomized comparison. Alternating days may be confounded by repeating activity schedules, and staff overrides were more common on delivery days. The two facilities also have similar wide corridors and are managed by the same operator. Badge participation excluded residents who declined monitoring or could not wear a badge consistently, while repeated encounters from the same residents make the regression confidence interval appear more precise than a resident-level analysis might. Finally, a pause can represent caution, conversation, fatigue, or waiting for another person; it should not automatically be interpreted as fear of the cart. Resident interviews would be needed to determine whether the movement changes correspond to a better corridor experience.
planted_strengths: Uses a specific, operationally meaningful question about robot yielding behavior rather than discussing elder care robotics in general terms.
Provides transparent sample construction, outcome definitions, subgroup counts, exclusions, and both absolute and relative effect estimates.
Identifies a meaningful heterogeneous pattern by mobility aid and reports a restricted one-encounter-per-resident-per-day check.
Includes countervailing operational evidence: early yielding reduces hesitation but increases doorway obstruction and route time.

planted_weaknesses: The alternating-day firmware schedule is not randomized or concealed and may be confounded by recurring schedules, staff behavior, delivery loads, or resident mix.

The primary regression clusters by day rather than resident despite repeated encounters, likely producing an overly narrow confidence interval; the restricted calculation does not provide a corrected inferential model.
The two facilities share an operator and similar layouts, sharply limiting external validity, yet the operational recommendation is somewhat firmer than the evidence warrants.
The hesitation definition combines pauses and lateral movement into a threshold-based proxy that cannot distinguish discomfort from benign waiting, fatigue, conversation, or other corridor traffic.

quality_rationale: The write-up is clear, numerically coherent, and unusually attentive to an overlooked interaction between robot navigation rules and residents’ walking continuity. It reports subgroup results, operational costs, sensor validation, and several limitations. Its causal credibility is only moderate, however: assignment alternated predictably by day, repeated encounters are handled inadequately in the main uncertainty estimate, missing encounters may be informative, and the behavioral proxy is easy to overinterpret. The recommendation is plausible but somewhat stronger and broader than a two-site observational comparison supports. These substantive merits and flaws place it near the middle of the scale.
